Say you are given the following tools:

A tool that searches the internet for relevant API calls.
A tool that executes an API call, in string form.

How would you then go about the process of ordering me a burger and fries from McDonald's.

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

message.content:
Below is a high‑level “recipe” for how you could use the two tools you described to place a McDonald’s order for a burger and fries.  
(Assume the tools are named `search_api` and `execute_api`.)

---

## 1. Find the McDonald’s ordering API

**Goal:** Discover the public (or at least discoverable) API endpoints that let you query the menu, add items to a cart, and place an order.

| Step | Action | Tool | Example |
|------|--------|------|---------|
| 1.1 | Search the web for “McDonald’s API” or “McDonald’s mobile ordering API” | `search_api` | `search_api("McDonald's mobile ordering API")` |
| 1.2 | Inspect the returned links for official documentation or SDKs | manual | Look for URLs like `https://developer.mcdonalds.com` or `https://api.mcdonalds.com`. |
| 1.3 | If no public API exists, look for third‑party wrappers (e.g., “McDonald’s API wrapper”, “McDonald’s REST API”) | `search_api` | `search_api("McDonald's REST API wrapper")` |

> **Tip:** Many fast‑food chains expose their APIs only to partners, so you may need to reverse‑engineer the mobile app’s network traffic or use a service like Postman’s “Capture Requests” feature.

---

## 2. Understand the API contract

Once you have a candidate endpoint:

| Step | Action | Tool | Example |
|------|--------|------|---------|
| 2.1 | Read the API spec (OpenAPI/Swagger, GraphQL schema, or raw docs) | manual | Download the Swagger JSON or read the README. |
| 2.2 | Identify required headers (e.g., `Authorization`, `X-Device-ID`) | manual | Note any mandatory fields. |
| 2.3 | Note the authentication flow (OAuth2, API key, JWT, etc.) | manual | Determine if you need to obtain a token first. |

---

## 3. Authenticate (if needed)

| Step | Action | Tool | Example |
|------|--------|------|---------|
| 3.1 | Call the auth endpoint to get a bearer token | `execute_api` | `execute_api({"url":"https://api.mcdonalds.com/auth/token","method":"POST","headers":{"Content-Type":"application/json"},"body":{"client_id":"…","client_secret":"…"}})` |
| 3.2 | Store the token for subsequent calls | internal | Keep the `access_token` in memory. |

---

## 4. Locate the nearest McDonald’s

| Step | Action | Tool | Example |
|------|--------|------|---------|
| 4.1 | Call the “locations” endpoint with your latitude/longitude | `execute_api` | `execute_api({"url":"https://api.mcdonalds.com/locations","method":"GET","params":{"latitude":40.7128,"longitude":-74.0060}})` |
| 4.2 | Parse the response to pick the closest store (by distance or ID) | manual | Choose the store with the smallest `distance` field. |

---

## 5. Retrieve the menu for that store

| Step | Action | Tool | Example |
|------|--------|------|---------|
| 5.1 | Call the “menu” endpoint with the store ID | `execute_api` | `execute_api({"url":"https://api.mcdonalds.com/menu","method":"GET","params":{"store_id":"12345"}})` |
| 5.2 | Scan the JSON for items named “Burger” and “Fries” (or their SKU codes) | manual | Note the `item_id` for each. |

---

## 6. Create a new cart / order

| Step | Action | Tool | Example |
|------|--------|------|---------|
| 6.1 | POST to `/cart` or `/order` to start a new session | `execute_api` | `execute_api({"url":"https://api.mcdonalds.com/cart","method":"POST","headers":{"Authorization":"Bearer …"},"body":{"store_id":"12345"}})` |
| 6.2 | Capture the returned `cart_id` or `order_id` | internal | Save the ID for later. |

---

## 7. Add items to the cart

| Step | Action | Tool | Example |
|------|--------|------|---------|
| 7.1 | POST each item to `/cart/{cart_id}/items` | `execute_api` | `execute_api({"url":"https://api.mcdonalds.com/cart/abc123/items","method":"POST","headers":{"Authorization":"Bearer …"},"body":{"item_id":"burger_001","quantity":1}})` |
| 7.2 | Repeat for fries | same as above | `item_id":"fries_001"` |

---

## 8. Checkout / finalize the order

| Step | Action | Tool | Example |
|------|--------|------|---------|
| 8.1 | POST to `/checkout` with payment details (card token, address, etc.) | `execute_api` | `execute_api({"url":"https://api.mcdonalds.com/cart/abc123/checkout","method":"POST","headers":{"Authorization":"Bearer …"},"body":{"payment_token":"tok_visa_123","delivery_address":"123 Main St"}})` |
| 8.2 | Receive confirmation (order number, ETA) | internal | Print or log the response. |

---

## 9. Error handling & retries

* Wrap each `execute_api` call in a try/catch block.
* If a 401 appears, re‑authenticate.
* For 429 (rate limit), back‑off exponentially.
* Log all responses for debugging.

---

## 10. Optional: Webhook / status polling

If the API supports it, register a webhook to receive updates on order status, or poll `/order/{order_id}` until the status changes to “completed”.

---

### Summary Flow

```
search_api → find API docs
parse docs → identify endpoints & auth
execute_api(auth) → token
execute_api(locations) → store_id
execute_api(menu) → item_ids
execute_api(cart) → cart_id
execute_api(add_item) × 2 → add burger & fries
execute_api(checkout) → order confirmed
```

With this skeleton you can plug in the actual URLs, headers, and payloads once you’ve discovered the real McDonald’s API (or a suitable third‑party wrapper). The two tools—search for the right endpoints and execute the calls—cover the entire ordering workflow.
